summary:
Mission to the South of the Moon is a desktop app that helps choose where and when to land at the lunar south pole. For each of NASA’s 13 Artemis III candidate regions, it uses NASA/JPL ephemerides and real LRO LOLA terrain to show, for any moment, whether the Sun (solar power) and Earth (direct communication) are visible above the local mountains. It then scores the landing day as optimal, acceptable or not optimal.

Working backwards from the landing date, it checks whether a rocket can launch from a real US pad at the right time, recommends a travel time, and lists only launches that are possible and land on an optimal day.

A 3D view shows the Sun, Earth and Moon to scale, and the Lander view shows the real terrain and its shadows. An ESP32 model points at the Sun and Earth, and the app makes a PDF trip report in one click.

This matters because at the pole a single ridge can cut power or contact for days. The app turns that complex geometry into a clear, checkable decision.
details:
What it does. Mission to the South of the Moon helps mission planners choose where and when to land at the lunar south pole. For each of NASA’s 13 Artemis III candidate regions, and for any date from 1902 to 2049, it shows whether the Sun (solar power) and Earth (direct radio contact) are in view from the surface. It scores the 24 hours after landing from 0 to 100 (optimal, acceptable or not optimal) and colours every day of the calendar by that score. It then works backwards from the landing date: it checks whether a rocket can launch from a chosen pad (Kennedy LC-39B/39A, Cape Canaveral, Wallops, Vandenberg) at the right time, recommends a travel time, and lists only the launches in the next 30 days that are both possible and land on an optimal day. A one-click PDF report sums up the trip.

How it works.

  • Sun, Earth and Moon positions come from the NASA/JPL DE421 ephemerides and NAIF lunar orientation kernels. Our results match NASA SVS “Moon Phase and Libration 2026” within 0.001°.
  • For each site, we compute the real horizon from LRO LOLA elevation data up to 300 km away, including the Moon’s curvature. A body counts as hidden when terrain blocks its disc.
  • Launch feasibility is a geometric check. The rocket’s parking-orbit plane must contain the Moon at arrival, on a launch heading the pad allows (Eastern Range 37°–112°, Western Range 147°–201°, Wallops 90°–160°). The model correctly marks the real Artemis II launch time (1 April 2026, 22:35 UTC, LC-39B) as possible.
  • Travel time is Artemis II’s real time, scaled with the Earth–Moon distance on arrival (Kepler’s third law).
  • An interactive 3D view shows the Sun, Earth and Moon to scale, with real Hipparcos stars. A Lander view shows the real terrain and its shadows, including partial sunrise behind ridges. A south pole map shows live sunlight and where Earth is visible.
  • A physical model, built on an ESP32 with motors and a servo, receives the Sun and Earth positions over Bluetooth Low Energy and points at them.

Benefits. At the south pole the Sun and Earth stay close to the horizon, so a ridge a few kilometres away can cut power or communication for days. The app turns this hard 3D geometry into a simple answer: land here, on this day, launch then. It also shows why, with views and numbers that anyone can check.

What we hope to achieve. We want a clear, trustworthy tool for students, educators and mission enthusiasts to explore Artemis landing choices. It can be extended with higher-resolution polar terrain (5–20 m LOLA mosaics) and more mission rules.

Tools and technologies. Python, PyQt6 / Qt WebEngine, three.js (WebGL, custom shaders, Web Workers), Skyfield, NumPy, bleak (Bluetooth LE), MicroPython on ESP32, PCA9685 and DRV8833 drivers, pytest (44 automated tests).

Two checks before you submit:

  • AI: if the form has a “Use of Artificial Intelligence” field, mention that you built the project with help from an AI assistant. Space Apps asks for this.
  • Travel time source: the Artemis II travel time currently comes from Wikipedia. If you want only NASA sources, replace it with NASA’s Artemis II mission page first.
